You are fixing TWO bugs in the Python repository checked out at /dateutil (the `python-dateutil` library), both in /dateutil/dateutil/rrule.py. Work only in /dateutil. Do NOT modify, delete, or weaken any existing test in /dateutil/dateutil/test/ — that is strictly forbidden. Verify with manual python snippets instead of adding tests.

BUG REPORT 1 (from a user):
"I wanted a yearly recurrence with no occurrences, so I passed count=0 and then asked how many dates it contains. I expected an empty result and a count of 0, but it gave me one date instead.
    rr = rrule(YEARLY, count=0, dtstart=datetime(1997, 9, 2, 9, 0))
    print(rr.count())   # prints 1, expected 0
"
So a rule with count=0 must yield no occurrences at all: `list(rrule(YEARLY, count=0, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)))` should be `[]` and `.count()` should be 0. Look at the `rrule` class (the `_iter` generator and the `count()` method) and fix the count=0 handling minimally. Be careful not to break count=None (infinite) or count>0 behavior, and not to break `rrule` with `until`.

BUG REPORT 2 (from a user):
"I was building an iCalendar string from a recurrence rule and noticed the `RRULE:` label was missing. For example:
    rule = rrule(YEARLY, count=5, dtstart=datetime(1997, 9, 2, 9, 0))
    print(str(rule))
I expected the output to be `DTSTART:19970902T090000` followed by `RRULE:FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5`. Instead I got `DTSTART:19970902T090000` followed by `FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5`. The same thing happens when I parse a string that already contains `RRULE:` and print it back: the `RRULE:` prefix disappears."
So `str(rrule(...))` must include the `RRULE:` prefix on the second line (and the `rrule.__str__` / `_rrule.__str__` implementation should be consistent). Look at `_rrule.__str__` in /dateutil/dateutil/rrule.py. Note the class also parses input strings that may or may not start with `RRULE:` — parsing must keep working for both forms (see `_rrulestr` / `rrule.__init__` handling of the `rrule` string argument and `_parse_rfc_rrule`). Make the minimal change so that str() output has the RRULE: prefix, and check the existing tests to see what format they expect (read the tests but do NOT edit them).

Verify with snippets:
  python -c "from datetime import datetime; from dateutil.rrule import rrule, YEARLY; r=rrule(YEARLY, count=5, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)); print(str(r)); print(list(r)); print(rrule(YEARLY, count=0, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)).count())"
Also verify round-tripping: `str(rrule(str(r)))` still works, and parsing a bare 'FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5' string still works.
Then run `python -m pytest dateutil/test/test_rrule.py -q` and report results (do not edit tests; if an existing test fails, report it and reconsider your change so that pre-existing tests keep passing — the RRULE: prefix expectation is documented in docs/rrule.rst, check it).

Report back: files changed (exact diff), verification commands and outputs, and test results.

BUG REPORT (from a user of the library):
"I was building a date by adding a whole-number float, for example `datetime(2000, 1, 1) + relativedelta(months=1.0)`. I expected this to behave just like `months=1` and produce `datetime(2000, 2, 1)`, because 1.0 is a whole number. Instead it raised `ValueError: Non-integer years and months are ambiguous and not currently supported.` The same thing happens with `years=1.0`, which is surprising when the value has no fractional part."

So: relativedelta(months=1.0) and relativedelta(years=1.0) should be accepted and behave exactly like months=1 / years=1. Genuinely fractional values (e.g. months=1.5, years=0.5) must still raise ValueError with the same message (that behavior is documented/expected).

Investigate /dateutil/dateutil/relativedelta.py (look at __init__ and the check that raises the ValueError) and implement the minimal fix. Note the check should use exact whole-number detection (e.g. `int(x) == x` / `x % 1 == 0`) rather than something that fails for floats.

Verify with snippets like:
  python -c "from datetime import datetime; from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta; print(datetime(2000,1,1)+relativedelta(months=1.0)); print(datetime(2000,1,1)+relativedelta(years=1.0))"
and confirm months=1.5 / years=0.5 still raise ValueError. Also run the existing test files `python -m pytest dateutil/test/test_relativedelta.py -q` (and test_rrule.py, test_parser.py if quick) and make sure nothing that passed before now fails.

Report back: files changed (with the exact diff), the verification commands and their outputs, and the test results.

You are verifying fixes in the Python repository at /dateutil (python-dateutil). Do NOT edit any file in /dateutil (read-only verification). A pristine baseline copy exists at /tmp/baseline_dateutil (identical to /dateutil before the fixes); you may read it for comparison but do not modify it.

Three fixes were just applied:
1. /dateutil/dateutil/relativedelta.py: whole-number floats for years/months are normalized to int (relativedelta(months=1.0) == relativedelta(months=1)); genuinely fractional values still raise ValueError.
2. /dateutil/dateutil/rrule.py: rrule with count=0 now yields no occurrences and count() == 0.
3. /dateutil/dateutil/rrule.py: str(rrule(...)) now includes the 'RRULE:' prefix on the second line.

Your job:
(a) Show `cd /dateutil && git diff` (full diff of the working tree) so the exact changes are visible.
(b) Run the full test suite: `cd /dateutil && python -m pytest dateutil/test -q --tb=short 2>&1 | tail -30`. Compare to the baseline result (1064 passed, 43 skipped, 0 failed). Report any newly failing test ids.
(c) Run the user's three exact reproduction snippets and show output:
  python -c "from datetime import datetime; from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta; print(datetime(2000,1,1)+relativedelta(months=1.0)); print(datetime(2000,1,1)+relativedelta(years=1.0))"
  python -c "from datetime import datetime; from dateutil.rrule import rrule, YEARLY; rr=rrule(YEARLY, count=0, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)); print(rr.count()); print(list(rr))"
  python -c "from datetime import datetime; from dateutil.rrule import rrule, YEARLY; rule=rrule(YEARLY, count=5, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)); print(str(rule))"
(d) Check edge cases / regressions around the changes:
  - relativedelta(months=1.5) and relativedelta(years=0.5) still raise ValueError with the message 'Non-integer years and months are ambiguous and not currently supported.'
  - relativedelta(months=1.0) + timedelta, -relativedelta(months=1.0), relativedelta(months=1.0).normalized(), relativedelta(years=1.0)*2, Decimal('1.0') input, relativedelta(dt1=..., dt2=...) still works.
  - rrule count=None still infinite; count=5 unchanged; until-only rules unchanged; rruleset containing a count=0 rule; rrule(...).replace(count=0).
  - Round-trip: `from dateutil.rrule import rrulestr; s = str(rrule(YEARLY, count=5, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0))); print(s); print(str(rrulestr(s))); print(list(rrulestr(s)) == list(rrule(YEARLY, count=5, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0))))` and parsing a bare 'FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5' string, and 'RRULE:FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5'.
  - Check `str(rruleset())` and a rruleset with an rrule added, to see whether the RRULE: prefix change affects rruleset.__str__ output (report what it prints; note whether it looks consistent).
  - Check that `rrulestr('DTSTART:19970902T090000\nRRULE:FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5')` still parses and that `rrulestr('FREQ=YEARLY;COUNT=5')` still parses.
(e) Report: full diff, test results (before/after comparison), each snippet's output, and any problem or regression found. Be concise but complete.

You are making a small, careful fix in the Python repository checked out at /dateutil (python-dateutil), file /dateutil/dateutil/rrule.py. Work only in /dateutil (temp files under /tmp are fine). Do NOT modify, delete, or weaken any existing test in /dateutil/dateutil/test/ — strictly forbidden.

Context: a previous fix made `rrule(..., count=0)` yield no occurrences (empty list, count() == 0). But `rrule.__str__` (around line 692) still uses `if self._count:` to decide whether to emit the COUNT=... part, so a rule with count=0 prints `DTSTART:...\nRRULE:FREQ=YEARLY` with no COUNT, and round-tripping that string through `rrulestr` produces an unbounded rule. This is inconsistent with the documented behavior of `__str__` (its docstring says: 'Output a string that would generate this RRULE if passed to rrulestr.') and with the new count=0 semantics.

Task: change the condition so that an explicit count of 0 is emitted, i.e. `if self._count is not None:` instead of `if self._count:`. Check whether any other place in rrule.py has the same truthiness problem for count (search for `_count`), and report but only change what is clearly the same defect. Do not change anything else.

Verify:
  python -c "from datetime import datetime; from dateutil.rrule import rrule, YEARLY, rrulestr; r=rrule(YEARLY, count=0, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)); print(repr(str(r))); print(list(rrulestr(str(r)))); print(rrulestr(str(r)).count())"
Expected: str(r) contains 'COUNT=0', and rrulestr of it yields [] and count 0.
Also check count=None (no COUNT emitted), count=5 (COUNT=5 emitted), and that `str(rrule(YEARLY, dtstart=datetime(1997,9,2,9,0)))` has no COUNT.
Then run `cd /dateutil && python -m pytest dateutil/test/test_rrule.py -q` and the full suite `python -m pytest dateutil/test -q` and report results (expected: 1064 passed, 43 skipped, 0 failed). Do not edit tests; if an existing test fails, report it and reconsider the change.

Report back: the exact diff, verification outputs, and test results.

You are fixing a bug in the Python repository checked out at /dateutil (the `python-dateutil` library), in /dateutil/dateutil/relativedelta.py. Work only in /dateutil (temp files under /tmp are fine). Do NOT modify, delete, or weaken any existing test in /dateutil/dateutil/test/ — strictly forbidden. The full pre-existing test suite currently passes: `cd /dateutil && python -m pytest dateutil/test -q` -> 1064 passed, 43 skipped, 0 failed. It must still pass after your change.

BUG REPORT (from a user):
"When I add two `relativedelta` objects together, any absolute value I set to zero vanishes from the result.
    >>> relativedelta() + relativedelta(day=0, hour=0)
    relativedelta()
    >>> relativedelta(day=0, hour=0) + relativedelta()
    relativedelta()
I expected both of these to keep `day=0` and `hour=0`, since I set them explicitly, but the sum comes back with no day or hour at all, as though I had never passed them. It happens no matter which side the zero-valued delta is on, so I can't combine deltas that deliberately pin a value to zero."

Root cause: `relativedelta.__add__` (in /dateutil/dateutil/relativedelta.py) builds the result with expressions like `day=self.day or other.day`, `hour=self.hour or other.hour`, etc. Because `0 or None` evaluates to `None`, an explicitly-set absolute value of 0 is lost. The fix: choose the value based on `is not None` rather than truthiness (e.g. `self.day if self.day is not None else other.day`), for all the absolute fields (year, month, day, weekday, hour, minute, second, microsecond). Note the relative fields (years, months, days, hours, minutes, seconds, microseconds, leapdays) are summed with `+` and should keep their current behavior. Also check `__radd__`/`__sub__`/`__rsub__` and any similar `or`-based logic in the file for the same defect and fix consistently if it is clearly the same bug (report what you changed).

Be careful about the intended semantics: the docstring of `relativedelta` says the result of adding two deltas is a delta that adds both; for absolute values, when both are set the more specific/other one wins (the existing `or` chain gives `self` priority). Keep that priority, just make it None-aware.

Verify with snippets:
  python -c "from dateutil.relativedelta import relativedelta; print(relativedelta() + relativedelta(day=0, hour=0)); print(relativedelta(day=0, hour=0) + relativedelta()); print(relativedelta(day=0) + relativedelta(day=5)); print(relativedelta(day=5) + relativedelta(day=0))"
Expected: first two keep day=0, hour=0; the last two should follow the existing priority rule.
Also verify that adding deltas still works for the usual cases: `relativedelta(years=1, day=15) + relativedelta(months=2)`, `relativedelta(hour=3) + relativedelta(minute=4)`, `relativedelta(weekday=MO) + relativedelta(day=1)`, and that `datetime(2000,1,1) + (relativedelta(day=0) + relativedelta())` behaves the same as before for non-zero values.
Then run `cd /dateutil && python -m pytest dateutil/test/test_relativedelta.py -q` and the full suite `python -m pytest dateutil/test -q` and report results. Do not edit tests; if an existing test fails, report it and adjust your fix so pre-existing tests keep passing.

Report back: files changed (exact diff), verification commands and outputs, and test results.

BUG REPORT 1 (from a user):
"I ran `parse("http://biz.yahoo.com/ipo/p/600221.html", fuzzy_with_tokens=True)` and expected it to pull the date out of the URL while giving me back the leftover text, like `(datetime(2060, 2, 21, 0, 0, 0), ('http://biz.yahoo.com/ipo/p/', '.html'))`. Instead the result was wrong: the `p` in the path was treated as a time-of-day marker, so the returned datetime had an hour of 1 instead of 0, and that `p` was missing from the skipped tokens. I only want fuzzy parsing to skip unrecognized text and still return the correct date and the full leftover string."

Root cause hint: in fuzzy parsing, the AM/PM handling (look for the `_ampm` regex, something like `(?P<ampm>[AaMmPp]{1,2})`, and the code that checks `l[i].lower() in ('am', 'pm')` / sets `hour = 1`) matches a bare 'p' or 'a' inside ordinary words/URLs. A single 'a'/'p' should not be treated as an AM/PM marker; only real am/pm tokens should. Look at how the regex is defined and how it is used, and make the minimal fix so that a lone 'a'/'p' is not interpreted as AM/PM (e.g. require the token to be exactly 'am'/'pm' or a real am/pm form). Be careful to keep all existing behavior for genuine 'am'/'pm' input and to keep the pre-existing tests passing (read dateutil/test/test_parser.py, do NOT edit it).

BUG REPORT 2 (from a user):
"I was parsing timestamps that sometimes end with a trailing colon, so I called `parse('2017-07-17 06:15:', fuzzy=True)`. I expected the trailing colon to be ignored and to get back `datetime(2017, 7, 17, 6, 15)`. Instead it crashed with an `IndexError: list index out of range`."

Reproduce: `python -c "from dateutil.parser import parse; print(parse('2017-07-17 06:15:', fuzzy=True))"` -> IndexError. Find the cause (likely in the fuzzy token-skipping loop in `_parse`, where an empty token after the colon is looked up in `self.info.jump` / `l[i]` without bounds checking) and fix it minimally so the trailing colon is simply skipped and the parse succeeds. Make sure other fuzzy inputs (including ones with trailing separators, e.g. '2017-07-17 06:15: ', '06:15:00', '2017-07-17 06:15:00') still behave sensibly.

Verify with snippets:
  python -c "from dateutil.parser import parse; print(parse('http://biz.yahoo.com/ipo/p/600221.html', fuzzy_with_tokens=True)); print(parse('2017-07-17 06:15:', fuzzy=True))"
Expected: `(datetime.datetime(2060, 2, 21, 0, 0), ('http://biz.yahoo.com/ipo/p/', '.html'))` and `2017-07-17 06:15:00`.
Then run `cd /dateutil && python -m pytest dateutil/test/test_parser.py -q` and the full suite `python -m pytest dateutil/test -q`, and report results. Do not edit tests; if an existing test fails, report it and adjust your fix so pre-existing tests keep passing.

Report back: files changed (exact diff), verification commands and outputs, and test results.
